title: A power mean turns a loss into a dial between average and worst case, and scaling decides which variable owns the gradient
summary: When a model has several outputs, the loss must combine their errors into one number. The power mean with exponent p is a family: p = 1 is the average, p = 2 the root mean square, larger p approaches the maximum, and p near 0 the geometric mean. The exponent changes which component the gradient listens to, and so does the scale of each variable: an unscaled large variable can own the whole gradient.

read_the_figure.question: With the same data and the same budget, does changing the objective change the answer, and by how much?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: time against signal, with the data and two fitted curves. Right: one bar per objective, the error of each fit against the true curve.
look_at: The three outliers: a classical objective is pulled towards them, a robust one is not.
The two curves: where they differ, the objective, not the data or the budget, made the difference.
The bars: the error against the known truth, which is only available for synthetic data.
The note on the budget: both fits had the same number of evaluations.
read_the_figure.proves: For this data set the choice of objective changes the fit as much as the bars show; it does not say which objective is best in general.
if_wrong: Scoring both fits by one of the two objectives, which favours it.
must_check: The score is independent of both objectives.
The truth used in the bars is stated.

terms.meaning: The p-th root of the average of the p-th powers of non-negative numbers.
The limit of the power mean as p goes to zero: the exponential of the average logarithm.
The limit as p goes to infinity: only the worst component counts.
The size of the model's miss in one output variable, in a chosen unit or scale.
The fraction of the gradient's weight that a component receives.
A typical size of a variable, used to divide it so that errors are comparable across variables.
The raw error divided by the scale of its variable.

remember: Power mean: $M_p=(\tfrac1n\sum e_i^p)^{1/p}$. $M_1$ is the mean, $M_2$ the RMS, $M_0$ the geometric mean, $M_{-1}$ the harmonic mean, $M_\infty$ the maximum.
$M_p$ increases with $p$: $\min\le M_{-1}\le M_0\le M_1\le M_2\le\dots\le\max$.
The gradient with respect to a component is $\partial M_p/\partial e_i=\tfrac1n M_p^{1-p}e_i^{p-1}$, so large errors receive weight growing like $e_i^{p-1}$.
With $p=1$ every component gets equal weight; with large $p$ the worst one gets nearly all.
Scale each variable first (divide by its typical size) or the variable with the largest numbers dominates every $p$.

understand.title: Easy: a dial from average to worst case
understand.text: Imagine four students with errors 1, 2, 5 and 10. The plain average ignores who is worst. Turn the dial up and the average increasingly cares about the single worst student, until at the top the answer is simply 10. Turn it down and it cares more about the best. The power mean is that dial, and the exponent $p$ is the knob.

understand.title: Medium: the exponent moves the gradient
understand.text: The derivative of the power mean with respect to a component is proportional to $e_i^{p-1}$. At $p=1$ all four students get the same share (0.25 each). At $p=2$ the shares are 0.06, 0.11, 0.28 and 0.56. At $p=4$ the worst gets 0.88 and at $p=8$ 0.99. Raising $p$ is equivalent to telling the optimiser to fix the worst component first.

understand.title: Hard: scale is a hidden exponent
understand.text: Suppose temperature is near 1000 and a species fraction near 0.01, and both are predicted with a 5 percent error. The squared errors are 2500 and $2.5\times10^{-7}$, so almost all of the gradient (a share of $1-10^{-10}$) belongs to temperature, whatever $p$ is, and the species is never learned. Dividing each variable by its scale makes both errors 0.05 and each gets half. Scaling and the exponent are two separate dials: scaling decides which variables are compared fairly, the exponent decides how much the worst is emphasised.

understand.title: Hardest: the dial changes what you are optimising
understand.text: A high $p$ is the right target if the worst component limits the use of the model, but its gradient is dominated by a few points and is noisy, and it is non-smooth in the limit. A low $p$ gives a smooth, stable gradient but accepts one bad component. A schedule that raises $p$ during training gets an easy start and a worst-case finish, and comparing models requires scoring them all with the same $p$ and scaling, not the one each was trained with.

steps.title: Definition and special cases
steps.tex: M_p(e)=\Big(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^{\,p}\Big)^{1/p},\quad M_1=\bar e,\ M_2=\text{RMS},\ M_0=\Big(\prod e_i\Big)^{1/n},\ M_\infty=\max_ie_i

steps.title: Monotone in p
steps.tex: p<q\ \Rightarrow\ M_p(e)\le M_q(e),\ \text{with equality only if all }e_i\text{ are equal}
steps.note: A consequence of Jensen's inequality applied to $x\mapsto x^{q/p}$. The values above rise steadily with $p$ and never exceed 10.

steps.title: The limit p to zero
steps.note: L'Hopital's rule on the logarithm. The geometric mean of 1, 2, 5, 10 is $100^{1/4}=3.162$, the entry at $p=0$.

steps.title: The gradient
steps.note: The share $w_i=e_i^{p-1}/\sum_je_j^{p-1}$ is the fraction of the total pull on component $i$. For $e=(1,2,5,10)$ the share of the worst is 0.25 at $p=1$, 0.556 at $p=2$, 0.882 at $p=4$ and 0.992 at $p=8$.

steps.title: Scaling decides who owns the gradient
steps.note: Take temperature near 1000 and a species fraction near 0.01 with 5 percent error each: raw errors 50 and 0.0005. For the squared loss the raw share of temperature is $1-10^{-10}$; after dividing by the scales both errors are 0.05 and each share is 0.5. The gradient magnitudes differ by $10^5$ before scaling.

steps.title: Choosing p
steps.tex: p=1:\ \text{typical error};\quad p=2:\ \text{least squares};\quad p\gg1:\ \text{worst component};\quad p\to0:\ \text{relative (multiplicative) error}
steps.note: Match the exponent to the failure that matters. A schedule that raises $p$ gradually combines a stable start with a worst-case finish. Always report the score with the same $p$ and scaling for all models compared.

worked.title: Dial the exponent on four errors and see who owns the gradient
worked.problem: Four output variables have normalised errors $e=(1,2,5,10)$. Compute $M_p$ for $p=1,2,4,8,\infty$ and the gradient share of each variable at $p=1,2,4,8$. Then take two raw errors, 50 for temperature and 0.0005 for a species, and give the squared-loss gradient shares before and after scaling by 1000 and 0.01.

solution.text: Raw squared-loss shares for temperature and species.

worked.answer: The dial moves the mean from 4.5 to 10 as $p$ goes from 1 to infinity, and the share of the worst variable from 25 percent to 99 percent by $p=8$. Without scaling, temperature has $1-10^{-10}$ of the gradient and the species is ignored; with scaling the two are equal.

analyze.q: Two models have equal RMS error. One has all errors equal, the other has one large and the rest small. How do their $M_8$ values compare, and what does that say about the choice of $p$?
Why does scaling by the typical size of each variable matter more than changing $p$ when variables differ by factors of $10^5$?
analyze.hint: Compare the effect of a factor $10^5$ with the effect of the exponent in the share.

analyze.q: With three outliers in the data (the F7.5 plot) which of $p=1,2$ or large $p$ would you expect to be most affected, and why?

evaluate.q: A study trains with $p=4$ and reports RMS error. Is the comparison with a $p=2$ model fair?
evaluate.hint: Which objective did each model optimise, and which one is scored?

evaluate.q: Is the geometric mean a good choice when one error can be zero?
evaluate.hint: What happens to the logarithm at zero?

checks.q: What does $p\to\infty$ do to the power mean?
checks.hint: Which component dominates the sum of $e^p$?
checks.answer: It tends to the largest error: only the worst component counts.

checks.q: Why does the gradient share of the worst component grow with $p$?
checks.answer: The weight of component $i$ is proportional to $e_i^{p-1}$, so with larger $p$ the ratio of the worst to the others, $(e_{\max}/e_j)^{p-1}$, grows geometrically.

checks.q: A learned model reports a small mean loss but one species has an error of 40 percent. Which exponent would reveal that?
checks.hint: Which $p$ is sensitive to the worst component?
checks.answer: A high $p$ (or the maximum of the normalised errors): the mean hides one bad component among many good ones.

checks.q: How would you scale variables that span many decades, such as concentrations from $10^{-12}$ to 1?
checks.answer: Work with logarithms of the concentrations (or divide by the local value), so every decade carries the same weight, and keep a floor to avoid taking the logarithm of zero.
